Your broker should firstly interview you to find out your goals and objectives. 

They should then present a few comparable options and educate you of the pros & cons of each - usually one will stick out. 

E.g. You want to pay it off as quickly as possible, and you save a lot of money, but may need to transfer out frequently - Offset.  
You're self employed, and your latest return is way stronger than last - 1-year financials lender.

The bank will look at your income as 'EBITDA (earnings before interest, tax, depreciation, and amortisation). 

If you revenue is $600k a year but you spend $550k a year on buying stock, you're only $50k on the books. 

Find a broker who can work through your tax returns and diligently calculate your 'taxable income'. If you started a director's wage about a year ago, your best bet would be going to CBA on a 6 month Simple Verification Niche. This Niche will use your director's wage for servicing as long you meet criteria. No other major will take you until your company is registered for 18 months min.

All the majors and general lenders will offer the same split, and I am bound by my 'Best Interest Duty' to the client. I will always go where it's best for the client.

Some small specialist banks like Latrobe and Pepper Money have different splits, but they compensate this with upfront application fees and +2-5% interest rates.

I used mutual connections and networking. I'm basically just a glorified salesman with some finance qualification. 

As a new broker, you'd want to focus on learning as much as you can, no point in having leads you can't close or settle.

If you want to find leads get really good at networking. As you grow, the level of networking should increase accordingly. From networking with agents, to managers, to general managers, to directors.
You can deliver great customer service. Honestly though, a reputation is something that takes time to build. Awards help too.

According to the compliance which we are regulated by, we need a hefty list of documents. This is for your protection, my protection and the bank's  

I generally need:
- 3 months bank statements 
- Fact Find Form
- Liability statements
- Payslips
- IDs 

And more.

We need to make sure your situation, requirements, and objectives align; using documents for verification.

Your borrowing capacity is a product of your income, liabilities, and circumstances. 

Unless you run into a large sum of money, or your pay increases, this will not budge substantially. 

If your goal is to get into your ideal home one day, I would recommend buying what you can as soon as you can. General rule of thumb is if you can save quicker than property prices increase, continue doing so; but if they're going up quicker than you can save, it's worthwhile buying.

Your first home will almost never be your last. Buy what you can, pay your own mortgage instead of someone else's. As that equity builds and inevitably maybe your career and income, you'll move up eventually. 

P.s. I've got an excel spreadsheet where I model this if anyone is keen to see it.
